adds.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
adds.summary: Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing today: Media Spokesperson/Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake (Oct 2024) said current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, and separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case-by-case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it go through a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, weighing inmate preference. Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

adds.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
adds.summary: The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

records.note: No statutory prison-placement rule found for Sri Lanka; prisons are sex-segregated male/female wards and placement is discretionary with medical assessment (Prisons Dept., Oct 2024). Rights group (CPRP) calls for dedicated transgender sections in current and future prisons, restated Feb 2026 (ceylontoday.lk — not independently fetchable, 403), indicating no dedicated units exist. Additional source for background: US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report (state.gov PDF) notes new police guidelines to stop arrest/harassment of transgender persons, but nothing on housing.

no prison-housing data found — searches for Mongolian trans-prisoner placement, detention and prison policy returned only generic international guides (PRI/Penal Reform International placement guide, UNDP good-practices mapping) with no Mongolia-specific content. Two rounds of web search (incl. UN/OHCHR SOGI coverage for the May 2026 country visit and the Advocates for Human Rights UPR submission Apr 2025) found nothing on trans prisoner housing, special units, or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for this jurisdiction.

adds.title: Trans Women in Ecuador's Prisons | PrisioTrans Human Rights Program
adds.summary: Silueta X (leading Ecuadorian trans-rights organisation), PrisioTrans program, documents 2011-2026: trans women in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers. Key cases: trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; 2022 complaint over cruel/inhuman/degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast/body implants; 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman drew calls for an independent investigation at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison. The program explicitly does NOT push a one-size placement rule, instead advocating individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

adds.title: Trans Women Report Being Punished for Their Identity in Ecuador Prisons (Spanish)
adds.summary: Pulitzer Center investigation: Ecuador's prisons are 'almost always male' - the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons (organisation Fundacion Vivir Libre says there are many more), and trans women are placed in male pavilions. Case: Venezuelan trans woman Alexa (27) detained Aug 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was initially sent to male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than the 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations (where many sexo-gender-diverse inmates are held); she received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The story documents rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity, showing placement practice operates by birth sex/legal sex with protective 'prioritaria' placement used unevenly.

records.note: Practice: trans women are housed in male facilities/pavilions in Ecuador's crisis-ridden prison system; no gender-identity placement rule is codified, and protective grouping (trans women kept together; 'prioritaria' pavilion for vulnerable inmates) is informal/uneven. An official SNAI human-rights manual with equality/non-discrimination approach exists (atencionintegral.gob.ec) and the July 2016 IACHR-welcomed move to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty set a framework, but placement remains discretionary per local orgs (Silueta X).

adds.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
adds.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

adds.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
adds.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

records.note: No Jamaican prison-housing policy, special custody units, or placement-by-gender-identity rule found; the system is sex-segregated with no legal gender recognition, and documented practice shows LGB/trans prisoners isolated (2018 UWI study) and subject to identity-targeted prisoner-on-prisoner violence (US State Dept 2023). Nothing located on solitary/administrative segregation specific to trans inmates.

adds.title: Protect transgender inmates'
adds.summary: Trinidad Express (Camille Hunte, 28 Nov 2018) on the official 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers (launched Nov 2018 by the CCJ, CAJO, UN Women, JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of TT): the Protocol states plainly that 'in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to use recommendations to prison authorities to ensure provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress. Official acknowledgment that housing placement for trans prisoners is discretionary, unsafe, and mediated only through sentencing recommendations - with no facility of its own.

records.note: Official judicial protocol (Nov 2018) confirms T&T's penal system has NO special facilities for trans/non-traditional-gender inmates; placement safety left to prison authorities via judicial recommendations at sentencing. No legal gender recognition exists (no mechanism to change gender marker), so male/female classification by birth certificate governs. No documented case of trans-specific solitary/administrative segregation or a dedicated custody unit found.

adds.title: Ghana parliament passes bill criminalising gay acts
adds.summary: BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities; it proposes that identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer be punished by up to three years' imprisonment, adds a 'duty to report' prohibited acts to police, and was passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required. Establishes the direct state pathway by which trans people in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone - the population to which any prison-placement practice would apply - while containing no provision on how such prisoners would be housed.

adds.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
adds.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison sentences of three to 10 years - up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer for promotion/advocacy. Community groups (e.g. One Love Sisters Ghana) report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. The article contains no information on prison placement of trans prisoners, confirming the absence of any publicly documented housing policy for them in Ghana.

records.note: No Ghana-specific prison-housing placement data found: no policy on placement by gender identity, no special custody units, no trans-specific solitary/segregation practice, and (given no legal gender recognition) binary male/female classification by law. The May 2026 Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill makes imprisonment of trans people for identity realistic (up to 3 yrs) - the antecedent to any placement question - but nothing documents where such prisoners would be housed. Existing coverage (US State Dept, HRW 2018) documents general prison abuse but not trans placement.
